ety.text: From Middle English nail, nayl, Old English næġl, from Proto-West Germanic *nagl, from Proto-Germanic *naglaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃nogʰ- (“nail”). Cognates Compare North Frisian Nail (“nail”), Saterland Frisian Nail (“nail”), West Frisian neil, German and Low German Nagel, Dutch and Swedish nagel, Danish and Norwegian Bokmål negl, Norwegian Nynorsk nagl, Finnish naula (“nail”), Estonian nael (“nail”), (compare Irish ionga, Latin unguis, Albanian nyell (“ankle, hard part of a limb”), Lithuanian nagas, Russian нога́ (nogá, “foot, leg”), но́готь (nógotʹ, “nail”), Ancient Greek ὄνυξ (ónux)…
From Middle English naylen, from Old English næġlan.

senses.d: The horny plate or appendage at the ends of the digits of various animals, including most reptiles, birds, and mammals (both nonhuman and human).
The thin, flat type of such a plate on the fingers and toes of humans, chimpanzees and some other primates.
ex: When I'm nervous I bite my nails.

senses.d: The basal thickened portion of the anterior wings of certain hemiptera.
The terminal horny plate on the beak of ducks and other allied birds.

A spike-shaped metal fastener used for joining wood or similar materials. The nail is generally driven through two or more layers of material by means of impacts from a hammer or other device. It is then held in place by friction.
ex: Yesterday my shirt got torn after I caught it on a nail.

senses.d: A round pedestal on which merchants once carried out their business, such as the four nails outside The Exchange, Bristol.
An archaic English unit of length equivalent to ¹⁄₂₀ of an ell or ¹⁄₁₆ of a yard (2+¹⁄₄ inches or 5.715 cm).
To fix (an object) to another object using a nail.
ex: He nailed the placard to the post.

senses.d: To drive a nail.
ex: He used the ax head for nailing.

senses.d: To stud or boss with nails, or as if with nails.
ex: The rivets of their arms were nail'd with gold.

senses.d: To catch.
ex: we'll nail the sophist to it, if we can get him on that charge;

senses.d: To expose as a sham.
To accomplish (a task) completely and successfully.
To hit (a target) effectively with some weapon.
Of a male, to engage in sexual intercourse with.
ex: There’s a benefit gala at the Boston Pops tonight, and... well, I’m trying to nail the flautist.

senses.d: To spike, as a cannon.
ex: That the Ordinance be not nayled, nor the munition fiered.

senses.d: To nail down: to make certain, or confirm.

Inherited from Old Spanish clavo, from Latin clāvus. The conservation of Latin /kl-/ is irregular (normally the result is /ʎ/, but cf. claro), which might imply a degree of Latin influence. Still, it is difficult to regard such a mundane term as learned or even semi-learned. First attested in the twelfth century.

ety.text: French naïvebor. English naive Borrowed from French naïve, feminine form of naïf, from Latin nātīvus (“native, natural”). Doublet of native.

senses.d: Lacking worldly experience, wisdom, or judgement; unsophisticated.
ex: I am sixteen going on seventeen, I know that I'm naive

senses.d: Not having been exposed to something.
Produced in a simple, childlike style, deliberately rejecting sophisticated techniques.
ex: By 1921 when Miró painted his key work, naive painting had been recognized by the avantgarde art world as a genre in its own right.

senses.d: Intuitive; designed to follow the way ordinary people approach a problem.
A naive person; a greenhorn.
ex: As a seasoned woman—of nineteen—I felt it was my place to tell each of these naïves that such plans were easier made than followed.
